title: Unit 1c - Arguments, Arrays, C-Strings Title Slide
summary: Title slide for CS103 Unit 1c covering arguments, arrays, and C-strings in C++. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This unit covers three major topics in C++ programming: function arguments (including pass-by-value and pass-by-reference), arrays (including sequential and random access patterns), and C-strings (character arrays). These concepts are foundational for understanding how data is passed between functions, how collections of data are stored and accessed in memory, and how text is represented in C/C++.
notes_text: This is the introductory slide for Unit 1c. The three topics covered here build upon basic I/O and expressions from earlier units and are essential for writing functions that manipulate collections of data.

title: Pass-by-Value, Local Variables, and Scope Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing a simplified view of pass-by-value, local variables, and scope concepts in C++.
main_text: This section provides a simplified view of how pass-by-value works in C++, along with an explanation of local variables and their scope. These concepts explain how data flows between functions and why modifications to parameters inside a function do not affect the caller's variables.
notes_text: This section header sets up the foundational understanding of function argument passing before diving into the more complex topic of pass-by-reference. Understanding pass-by-value is critical before learning about arrays and how they differ.

title: Motivating Question: What Does This Code Print?
summary: Presents a C++ code example asking what the output will be when a function attempts to decrement a passed-by-value argument.
main_text: The slide poses the question: What will this code print? The code declares a function void dec(int) and in main() sets int y = 3, calls dec(y), then prints y. The dec function takes int y as a parameter and decrements it with y--. The key insight is that since y is passed by value, the dec function operates on a copy of y, so the original y in main remains 3. The program will print 3, not 2. This motivates the discussion of pass-by-value semantics.
notes_text: This is a classic introductory example for pass-by-value. Students often expect the output to be 2, but because the argument is copied, the decrement in dec() only affects the local copy. The original variable in main() is unchanged.

images.description: Code block showing void dec(int) prototype, main() with int y=3, dec(y) call, cout statement, and the dec function body with y--

title: Argument Passing: Pass-by-Value Explained
summary: Explains pass-by-value as copying an argument to a function, analogous to emailing an attached document rather than sharing the original.
main_text: Passing an argument to a function makes a copy of the argument. In CS terminology, this is called pass-by-value. Pass-by-value is like e-mailing an attached document: you still have the original on your PC, the recipient has a copy which she can modify, but modifications will not be reflected in your version. Communication is essentially one-way: the caller communicates arguments to the callee, but these are copies. Any processing the callee does is not visible to the caller. The only communication back to the caller is via a return value.
notes_text: The email attachment analogy is powerful for understanding pass-by-value. Just as an email attachment creates an independent copy that the recipient can modify without affecting the original, pass-by-value creates an independent copy of data for the called function. The return value is the only mechanism for the callee to send information back.

images.description: Diagram showing caller() at top sending arguments (step 1) to callee() at bottom, with return value (step 2) going back up. Laptop and email icons illustrate the copy-and-send analogy.

title: Pass by Value (1): Arguments as Local Variables
summary: Demonstrates that function arguments act like local variables, receiving copies that are deallocated when the function ends.
main_text: Function arguments/parameters act like local variables to that function. They are only in scope (only live) in the function's curly braces and then get deallocated. When arguments are passed, a copy of the actual argument value (e.g. 3) is given to the function's input argument. So the function is operating on a copy and that copy will die when the function ends. The code example shows main() with int y = 3, calling dec(y), then printing y. The dec function receives its own copy of y, decrements it to 2, but this copy is destroyed when dec returns. Main's y remains 3.
notes_text: The visual metaphor of boxes within boxes (sandboxes) reinforces that each function has its own isolated memory space. The copy of y in dec() starts as 3, becomes 2 after y--, but is then destroyed. The original y in main() is never touched.

images.description: Diagram showing main's y=3 being copied into dec()'s sandbox where it becomes 2, but with a prohibition symbol showing the copy cannot affect the original. Code listing shown alongside.

title: Pass by Value (2): Same Name, Different Variables
summary: Clarifies that variables with the same name in different functions are completely separate entities, and return is the only way to communicate back.
main_text: Even though both main and dec have a variable named 'y', each function is a separate entity and so two 'y' variables exist (one in main and one in dec that decrements it). The only way to communicate back to main is via return. Students should try to change the code appropriately to make it work. Main Point: Each function is a completely separate sandbox (i.e. is isolated from other functions and their data) and copies of data are passed and returned between them. The code shows the original version that prints 3, and a fill-in-the-blank version asking students to fix it using return.
notes_text: This slide drives home function isolation. The solution requires changing dec to return the decremented value and main to capture it with y = dec(y). The sandbox metaphor is central to understanding C++ function semantics before learning about references and pointers.

images.description: Sandbox diagram showing main's y starting at 3 (later crossed out to show potential fix), dec()'s copy at 2, and a return value path of 2 going back to main. Two code listings shown: original and fill-in-blank version.

title: Formals and Actuals (1): Parameter Terminology
summary: Introduces the distinction between formal parameters (placeholders in function definition) and actual parameters (values passed by the caller).
main_text: Formal parameters are the placeholder names (n1 and n2) used internally by the function to refer to the values passed. They are similar to how generic placeholders/titles in contracts like 'President' or 'professor' will be assigned or replaced with real values. Actual parameters are the actual values to be passed (i.e. the values to be substituted for the placeholders, such as 'Abraham Lincoln' or 'Mark'). A copy is made and given to the function. The example shows double avg(int n1, int n2) where n1 and n2 are formals. In main, x=6 and y=9 are the actuals in z = avg(x,y), producing copies 6 and 9 for n1 and n2. The function computes sum = n1 + n2 = 15 and returns sum/2.0 = 7.5. Each type is a different shape (int = triangle, double = square, char = circle). Only a value of that type can fit as a parameter.
notes_text: The shape analogy (triangle for int, square for double, circle for char) helps students understand type matching between actuals and formals. When avg(x, 2) is called, the actual 2 is a literal integer that gets copied to n2.

images.description: Diagram showing actuals x=6 and y=9 being copied into formals n1 and n2 in the avg() sandbox, with return value 7.5. Code listing shows avg function and main calling it. An 'Average' form widget shown for visualization.

title: Formals and Actuals (2): Second Function Call
summary: Shows a second call to avg(x, 2) demonstrating that actual parameters can be variables or literals, with copies always made.
main_text: Continuing the formals and actuals example, this slide shows the second call z = avg(x, 2). The formal parameters are still n1 and n2, placeholder names used inside the function. The actual parameters are x (value 6) and the literal 2, passed to n1 and n2 on the second call. A copy is made and given to the function. The actuals 6 and 2 are copied into formals n1 and n2, the function computes sum = n1 + n2 = 8 and returns sum/2.0 = 3.0 (note: since n1+n2=8 and stored as double, 8/2.0=4.0 -- but the slide shows 3.0 for avg(6,2) which is actually 4.0). Each type is a different shape: int = triangle, double = square, char = circle. Only a value of that type can fit as a parameter.
notes_text: This reinforces that actual parameters can be either variables or literal values. The key is that a copy is always made regardless. The type-shape analogy continues to illustrate type safety in C++.

images.description: Diagram showing actuals x=6 and literal 2 being copied into formals n1 and n2 in the avg() sandbox, with return value. Code listing shows second call z = avg(x, 2).

title: Pass-by-Value and Pass-by-Reference: Email Analogy Introduction
summary: Poses the question of pros and cons of emailing a document as an attachment versus sending a link, setting up the pass-by-reference concept.
main_text: This slide asks students to consider the pros and cons of emailing a LARGE document by two methods: attaching it to the email, or sending a link (URL) to the document on some cloud service (e.g. Google Docs). This analogy sets up the distinction between pass-by-value (attachment/copy) and pass-by-reference (link to original). The question is left open for students to think about before the next slide provides the answer.
notes_text: This is a pedagogical setup slide using a real-world analogy students can relate to. Attachments are independent copies (pass-by-value), while links give direct access to the original (pass-by-reference). The tradeoffs involve data size, modification visibility, and efficiency.

images.description: Email icon with attachment clip and a Google Docs icon, representing the two methods of sharing a document.

title: Pass-by-Value and Pass-by-Reference: Definitions
summary: Defines pass-by-value as emailing a copy (attachment) and pass-by-reference as emailing a link to the original, where modifications are shared.
main_text: Building on the email analogy, this slide provides the key definitions. Pass-by-value is like emailing an attachment: a copy is made and sent. The recipient can modify their copy, but the original is unaffected. Pass-by-reference means emailing a link to the original document. No copy is made and any modifications by the other party are seen by the originator. This is the fundamental difference: pass-by-value creates independent copies while pass-by-reference gives direct access to the original data.
notes_text: This distinction is crucial for understanding how arrays work in C/C++. Pass-by-value is the default for scalar types (int, double, char), while arrays are always passed by reference. The link analogy maps directly to memory addresses/pointers.

images.description: Email icon with attachment clip representing pass-by-value, and Google Docs icon representing pass-by-reference.

title: Arrays and Pass-by-Reference
summary: Explains that single scalar variables are passed by value while arrays are passed by reference in C/C++, with addresses (links) passed instead of copies.
main_text: Single (scalar) variables are passed-by-value in C/C++: copies are passed, like email attachments. Arrays are passed-by-reference: links (addresses) are passed, like a link to a shared doc. Changes are made to the original argument, not a copy. Arrays need not be returned since the function is modifying the original. The diagram contrasts the two approaches: for scalar arguments, the caller sends a copy (step 1) and receives a return value (step 2). For array arguments, only a link/address is sent (step 1), and the callee can directly modify the caller's data.
notes_text: This is a key concept slide. The star icons indicate this is especially important material. Students must understand that when they pass an array to a function, the function can modify the original array's contents. This is fundamentally different from scalar pass-by-value behavior.

images.description: Two side-by-side diagrams comparing scalar argument passing (copy with return value) and array argument passing (link/address only). Stars emphasize importance.

title: Why Arrays Are Pass-by-Reference
summary: Explains that arrays are passed by reference to avoid copying potentially huge amounts of data, passing only a starting address instead.
main_text: If arrays were passed by value, we would have to make a copy of a potentially HUGE amount of data (what if the array had a million elements). This would be very bad for performance. To avoid copying vast amounts of data, we pass a link instead. The code example shows int sum(int data[], int size) which takes an array and its size. In main, int vals[100] is declared and sum(vals, 100) is called. The diagram shows main's vals array at addresses 7420-7516, and how if passed by value, all 100 elements would need to be copied. Instead, only the starting address 7420 is passed as the link.
notes_text: This explains the engineering rationale behind the design decision. Copying millions of elements would be prohibitively slow, so C/C++ passes the memory address instead. This also means the function can modify the original data, which is both a feature and a potential source of bugs.

images.description: Diagram showing main()'s vals array (addresses 7420-7516) with a prohibition symbol over a hypothetical copy, and the actual passing of just the address 7420 to sum()'s data parameter. Code listing shows the sum function.

title: What Is Actually Passed for Arrays: Starting Address
summary: Reveals that the 'link' passed for arrays is the starting address (pointer) in memory, and the function uses address, type, and index to access elements.
main_text: The 'link' that is passed is just the starting address of (pointer to) the array in memory (e.g. 7420). Once the function has the start address and the type, it will produce its own index values and be able to access the array in the caller's memory. To access an element in an array, we need 3 pieces of info: 1) Start address of the array, 2) Index/offset, 3) Type of elements in the array (really the size of that type). The code shows sum(int data[], int size) receiving the starting address 7420 for data. The diagram shows main's vals array and sum's data parameter both pointing to address 7420.
notes_text: This slide reveals the mechanism behind pass-by-reference for arrays. The function receives a memory address, and combined with the element type (which determines byte size) and an index, it can calculate the exact memory location of any element. This foreshadows pointer concepts covered later.

images.description: Diagram showing main's vals array at address 7420, with data in sum() receiving the value 7420 as a pointer/disk icon, enabling sum to access the same memory. Info box lists the 3 pieces needed for array element access.

title: Strange Question: Can You Determine Array Size From Its Address?
summary: Uses a houses-on-a-block analogy to show that knowing an array's starting address does not tell you its size, so size must be tracked separately.
main_text: The first house on a block of a street has address 7420. How many houses are on the block? You cannot tell just from the starting address. Similarly, an array starts at address 7420 in memory. How many elements are in that array? Having the start address does not allow us to know how big the array is. Looking at raw memory (shown as hex values at various addresses), there is no way to distinguish where the array ends. We must also track and pass the size. This motivates why C/C++ array functions always need a separate size parameter.
notes_text: This analogy effectively demonstrates a key limitation of C/C++ arrays compared to languages like Java or Python that track array length automatically. The memory table shows raw hex values at addresses 7412-7436+, illustrating that memory is just bytes with no inherent structure.

images.description: Photo of row houses on a street, used as analogy for contiguous memory. Memory table showing addresses 7412-7436 with hex data values.

title: Arrays in C/C++ vs Other Languages: Size Tracking
summary: Contrasts C/C++ arrays requiring manual size tracking with Java and other languages that provide built-in size properties.
main_text: If sum() only has the start address, it would not know how big the array is. Unlike Java or other languages where you can call some function or access some property to give the size of an array, C/C++ require you to track the size yourself in a separate variable and pass it as a secondary argument. The code shows int sum(int data[], int size) where size must be explicitly passed. In main, int vals[100] is declared and sum(vals, 100) is called with 100 as the size. The diagram shows main's vals array with the value 100 being passed alongside the address 7420 to sum's data and size parameters.
notes_text: This is a critical difference between C/C++ and higher-level languages. In Java, arrays have a .length property. In Python, len() works on lists. C/C++ have no such mechanism for raw arrays, making buffer overflows possible if the wrong size is passed.

images.description: Diagram showing main's vals array with both the address 7420 and size 100 being passed to sum()'s data and size parameters. Code listing shows the sum function with size parameter.

title: Pass-by-Value / Reference Complete Example
summary: Full code example demonstrating both pass-by-value for scalars and pass-by-reference for arrays, showing that only array modifications persist.
main_text: This slide shows a complete program demonstrating both pass-by-value and pass-by-reference. The program includes function prototypes: int initScalarInt(), void initArrayOfInts(int x[], int len), and void printVals(int x1, int x2[], int x2len). The initScalarInt function returns 42. The initArrayOfInts function sets all elements of array x to 42 using a for loop. In main, int x1 and int x2[5] are declared. Initial values are printed (showing garbage), then values are set: x1 = initScalarInt() and initArrayOfInts(x2, 5). After setting, values are printed again. The scalar x1 receives the return value 42, and the array x2 is modified directly since arrays are passed by reference.
notes_text: This comprehensive example lets students see both mechanisms side by side. x1 gets its value through a return statement (pass-by-value for scalars), while x2 is modified in-place by initArrayOfInts because arrays are passed by reference. The printVals function needs the array length passed separately.

images.description: Two code panels side by side: left panel shows function definitions (prototypes, initScalarInt, initArrayOfInts), right panel shows main() and printVals function

title: Array Tasks and Access Patterns Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing strategies and questions to determine coding approaches for array tasks and access patterns.
main_text: This section covers strategies and questions to ask to determine coding approaches for array-based problems. The two main access patterns are sequential access (iterating through all elements) and random access (computing a specific index to access one element). Understanding which pattern to use is crucial for writing efficient and correct array code.
notes_text: This section bridges the theoretical understanding of arrays with practical problem-solving. Students need to learn to identify which access pattern a problem requires before writing code.

title: Sequential vs Random Access
summary: Defines sequential access as iterating through all elements with loops and random access as computing one specific index to access directly.
main_text: Most array-based tasks fall into either a sequential-access pattern or random-access pattern. Sequential access iterates (loops) through all elements. It is used for tasks that require looking at all elements in the worst case. Random access computes the ONE index to access. It is used for tasks that only require accessing one specific element. The sequential example shows a scores array at addresses 520-1076 with indices [0]-[19], using a for loop with total += scores[i] to sum all elements. The random access example shows using a student ID (stuID = 2) to directly access scores[stuID] to get one specific score (93), with code: cin >> stuId; cout << scores[stuID];
notes_text: Sequential access uses a loop variable (typically i) that increments through all indices. Random access uses a computed or input-provided index to jump directly to one element. Many problems combine both patterns.

images.description: Two array diagrams: left shows sequential access with arrow sweeping across all elements and a for loop summing them; right shows random access with stuID=2 jumping directly to scores[2]=93

title: Sequential Access: Common Tasks
summary: Lists common tasks requiring sequential access: combining all elements (sum, count-if, modify-all) and searching/selecting elements.
main_text: Use sequential access when you MUST (or POTENTIALLY need to) visit EVERY element. Common tasks that require sequential access include: Combining ALL elements such as sum or average, count-if (e.g. count how many 100s), and modify-all (e.g. increment all). Search/select an element potentially stopping (break) early in an unsorted array, such as finding a particular value or finding the minimum/maximum. The diagrams show two examples: computing a sum by iterating left-to-right through scores[93, 84, 96, ..., 90] accumulating into a sum variable, and find(96) searching through the array left-to-right looking for the value 96.
notes_text: The distinction between tasks that must visit every element (sum, average) and tasks that may stop early (search, find) is important. Both use sequential access but the latter can use break to exit the loop early when the target is found.

images.description: Two array diagrams showing sequential access patterns: top shows summing all elements with rightward arrow across full array into sum variable; bottom shows find(96) searching left-to-right through the array

title: Random Access Motivation and Examples Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing random access motivation and examples for array-based problems.
main_text: This section covers the motivation for random access and provides examples of when and how to use arrays for direct element access via computed indices. Random access is used when you only need to visit one element and can compute its index directly.
notes_text: Random access is a powerful concept that enables lookup tables, frequency counting, and other applications where the index can be calculated from the input data.

title: Arithmetic Expressions: When No Array Is Needed
summary: Shows that when input-to-output relationships follow simple arithmetic patterns (like f(x) = 2x+1), no array is needed.
main_text: To understand random access, consider a series of problems of converting some input x to an output f(x). Some relationships can be easily expressed arithmetically and no array is needed. The example shows a mapping: x=0 maps to f(x)=1, x=1 to 3, x=2 to 5, x=3 to 7, x=4 to 9. This forms a linear relationship visible on the graph. The code reads x from input and should compute y using an arithmetic expression. Students are asked to determine f(x) and fill in the blank for y = ____;. The answer (shown on the next slide) is f(x) = 2*x + 1.
notes_text: This slide establishes a progression: first showing that simple patterns do not need arrays, then building to cases where arrays become necessary. The linear graph makes the 2x+1 pattern visually clear.

images.description: Input-output table showing x values 0-4 mapping to f(x) values 1,3,5,7,9. Line graph showing the linear relationship. Code snippet with blank for the expression. Flow diagram showing x->f(*)-> f(x).

title: Arithmetic Expressions Solution: f(x) = 2*x + 1
summary: Reveals the solution f(x) = 2*x + 1 for the arithmetic expression problem, showing the code y = 2*x + 1.
main_text: The solution to the arithmetic expression problem is f(x) = 2*x + 1. The code becomes: int x, y; cin >> x; y = 2*x + 1; cout << y << endl; This demonstrates that when a simple mathematical formula exists to convert input to output, no array is needed. The input-output table confirms: f(0)=1, f(1)=3, f(2)=5, f(3)=7, f(4)=9, all following the pattern 2x+1.
notes_text: This is the simplest case in the progression toward understanding when arrays are necessary. Arithmetic expressions work when there is a clean mathematical relationship between input and output.

images.description: Same input-output table and graph as previous slide, now with solution f(x) = 2*x + 1 shown and code filled in with y = 2*x + 1

title: Piece-wise Expressions: Using if..else
summary: Shows that some input-output mappings require piece-wise expressions with if..else statements when the relationship changes at certain thresholds.
main_text: Consider a series of problems of converting some input x to an output f(x). Some relationships can be easily expressed using piece-wise relationships with if..else statements. The example shows: x=0 maps to 1, x=1 to 3, x=2 to 5, x=3 to 7, x=4 to 7, x=5 to 7. The graph shows a linear increase up to x=3, then a flat line at 7 for x>=4. This is a piece-wise function: f(x) follows one formula for x<=3 and another for x>3. Students need to fill in the if condition and both branches of the code.
notes_text: This builds on the arithmetic expression case by showing what happens when one formula does not cover all cases. Piece-wise functions (if..else) handle this naturally. The next step will show cases where even piece-wise expressions are insufficient.

images.description: Input-output table showing x 0-5 mapping to f(x) 1,3,5,7,7,7. Graph showing linear rise then flat plateau. Code with blank if condition and two blank assignments.

title: Piece-wise Expressions Solution
summary: Reveals the solution: f(x) = 2x+1 if x<=3, otherwise f(x) = 7, implemented with an if..else statement.
main_text: The solution shows f(x) = 2x+1 if x <= 3, and f(x) = 7 otherwise. The code becomes: if(x <= 3) y = 2*x + 1; else y = 7; This piece-wise expression correctly handles the two regions of the function. For inputs 0-3, the linear formula applies. For inputs 4 and above, the output is constantly 7.
notes_text: The progression continues: some mappings are arithmetic (one formula), some are piece-wise (if..else with different formulas). The next case will show mappings that have no discernible pattern, requiring arrays as lookup tables.

images.description: Input-output table and graph with solution shown: f(x) = 2x+1 if x<=3, f(x) = 7 otherwise. Code filled in with the if..else solution.

title: Arbitrary Data: Array as a Lookup Table
summary: Demonstrates that when input-output mappings have no arithmetic pattern, arrays serve as lookup tables where y = f[x] directly retrieves the answer.
main_text: For arbitrary or data where patterns cannot easily be derived, simply store them in an array and 'look them up.' The example shows x=0 maps to 4, x=1 to 1, x=2 to 0, x=3 to 4, x=4 to 5, x=5 to 3. The scatter plot shows no clear pattern. The solution uses an array as a lookup table: int x, y, f[]={4,1,0,4,5,3}; cin >> x; y = f[x]; cout << y << endl; The input x serves directly as the array index, and f[x] gives the corresponding output. This is the key motivation for random access.
notes_text: This completes the progression from arithmetic to piece-wise to lookup table. When data is truly arbitrary with no formula, an array is the natural solution. The index IS the input, and the stored value IS the output. This is one of the most powerful uses of random access.

images.description: Input-output table showing arbitrary mapping, scatter plot with no pattern, code using array as lookup table, and array visualization showing f[] = {4,1,0,4,5,3}

title: Problem 1: Integer to Letter Conversion
summary: Practice problem: write a function to convert an integer position 1-26 to its corresponding letter 'a'-'z' using a lookup table or arithmetic.
main_text: Consider the letters of the alphabet 'a'-'z'. Write a function to convert an integer position (aka ordinal) 1-26 to its corresponding letter. The mapping shows: 1 maps to 'a', 2 maps to 'b', 3 maps to 'c', ..., 26 maps to 'z'. The solution uses a character array: char f[26]={'a', 'b', 'c', ... 'z'}; cin >> x; char y = f[x-1]; // or equivalently: char y = 'a'+x-1; The array approach uses f[x-1] since the array is 0-indexed but positions start at 1. The arithmetic approach uses character arithmetic: 'a'+x-1 works because characters are integers in ASCII.
notes_text: This problem has both an array solution and an arithmetic solution. The arithmetic approach exploits ASCII encoding where letters are consecutive. The -1 offset is needed because the problem uses 1-based numbering but arrays are 0-indexed.

images.description: Mapping table showing integers 1-26 going through function f to produce characters 'a'-'z'. Code showing both array and arithmetic solutions.

title: Problem 2: Survey Code to Word Conversion
summary: Practice problem converting survey codes (0=Yes, 1=No, 2=Unsure) to words using either if-else chains or an array lookup table.
main_text: A survey uses a code where 0 = 'Yes', 1 = 'No', 2 = 'Unsure'. Write a program to convert the code to the corresponding word. Two solutions are shown side by side. The if-else approach: if(x == 0) y = 'Yes'; else if(x == 1) y = 'No'; else if(x == 2) y = 'Unsure'; The array lookup approach: string y, f[] = { 'Yes', 'No', 'Unsure' }; y = f[x]; // what could go wrong? The comment 'what could go wrong?' hints at the danger of out-of-bounds access if x is not 0, 1, or 2. The array approach is more concise but requires input validation.
notes_text: This problem illustrates the tradeoff between if-else chains and lookup tables. The array approach is cleaner and more scalable but vulnerable to out-of-bounds access. This motivates bounds checking, an important practice in C/C++.

images.description: Mapping diagram showing 0->Yes, 1->No, 2->Unsure. Two code panels showing if-else solution and array lookup solution side by side.

title: Counting / Frequency Analysis / Histograms
summary: Introduces frequency counting as a common random-access application that combines sequential input reading with random-access array updates.
main_text: Another common use for random-access is applications involving counting, frequency analysis, or histograms. This often combines BOTH sequential and random-access patterns. Given a set of inputs, count the frequency (occurrences) of each result, or put them into bins and count how many fall in each bin. The example shows scores x: [84, 93, 88, 87, 96, 78] being classified into grade bins: 60-69 (index 0), 70-79 (index 1), 80-89 (index 2), 90-99 (index 3), 100 (index 4). The frequency array F[] starts at all zeros. As scores are processed sequentially, the appropriate bin is updated via random access: 84 goes to bin 2 (F[2] increments), then 93 to bin 3, etc. The final result: F[] = {0, 1, 3, 2, 0}.
notes_text: This is a very common pattern in programming: iterate through data sequentially, but use each data value to compute an index for random access into a counting array. This pattern appears in histograms, vote tallying, character frequency analysis, and many other applications.

images.description: Two-stage diagram showing scores array being processed left-to-right (sequential) while updating frequency bins (random access). Left shows initial state, right shows after processing all scores.

title: Input Range to Array Domain (1): Mapping Problem
summary: Identifies that input ranges (60-100) must be converted to valid array indices (0 to n-1) since arrays are 0-indexed.
main_text: Problem: The only valid array indexes are 0 to n-1 (i.e. the DOMAIN of an array is 0 to n-1). So in the histogram scenario we need to convert the RANGE of the inputs (60-100) to the ARRAY DOMAIN (0 to 4). The diagram shows two steps: for score 84, a function f converts it to index 2, mapping to the 80-89 bin. For score 78, f converts it to index 1, mapping to the 70-79 bin. The conversion function maps input values from their natural range to valid 0-based array indices. Each bin covers a decade: 60s map to 0, 70s to 1, 80s to 2, 90s to 3, 100 to 4.
notes_text: This is a crucial concept: the input data's range rarely matches the 0-based indexing of arrays. Students must learn to write conversion functions (arithmetic expressions) that map from the input domain to the array index domain.

images.description: Two diagrams showing scores 84 and 78 being converted through function f to array indices 2 and 1 respectively, updating frequency array F[]

title: Input Range to Array Domain (2): Conversion Techniques
summary: Shows that arithmetic expressions, piece-wise expressions, or even another array can convert input ranges to array indices.
main_text: To convert the RANGE of the inputs (60-100) to the ARRAY DOMAIN (0 to 4), we can use any of the techniques learned previously: arithmetic expression, piecewise expression, even another array as a lookup table (though this would be hard with such a large domain). The diagrams show the same mapping problem with f(x) = ___ left as a blank for students to determine. The conversion must map: 60-69 to 0, 70-79 to 1, 80-89 to 2, 90-99 to 3, 100 to 4.
notes_text: Students should recognize this as an integer division problem. Dividing the score by 10 gives the tens digit, and subtracting 6 shifts it to the 0-based range. The next slide provides the solution.

images.description: Same histogram diagrams as previous slide with conversion function f(x) = ___ shown as blank for students to solve

title: Input Range to Array Domain (2) Solution: f(x) = x/10 - 6
summary: Reveals the solution f(x) = x/10 - 6 for converting scores (60-100) to array indices (0-4) using integer division.
main_text: The solution for converting the input range 60-100 to array domain 0-4 is f(x) = x / 10 - 6. Using integer division: 84/10 = 8, 8-6 = 2 (correct index for 80s bin). 78/10 = 7, 7-6 = 1 (correct index for 70s bin). 93/10 = 9, 9-6 = 3 (correct index for 90s bin). 100/10 = 10, 10-6 = 4 (correct index for 100 bin). This arithmetic expression efficiently converts any score in the valid range to its corresponding bin index.
notes_text: Integer division is the key insight. x/10 extracts the tens digit (in integer arithmetic), and subtracting 6 shifts the range from 6-10 to 0-4. Students should verify this works for boundary values like 60, 69, 70, 99, and 100.

images.description: Histogram diagrams with solution f(x) = x/10 - 6 filled in, showing correct index calculations for sample scores

title: A Final Problem: Grade Mapping with Arrays
summary: Practice problem mapping quiz scores (0-10) to letter grades (A-F) using either a large lookup table or arithmetic conversion with a smaller table.
main_text: Suppose an instructor with 8 students gives a quiz worth 10 points and we use the customary grading scale (>90% = A, 80% = B, 70% = C, 60% = D, <60% = F). We want to map the points to the letter grade. The grade scale: 0-49 = F, 50-59 = F, 60-69 = D, 70-79 = C, 80-89 = B, 90-99 = A, 100 = A. Two approaches are shown: Left approach uses a large grades array with 11 entries (one per possible score 0-10): grades[11] = {'F','F','F','F','F','F','D','C','B','A','A'} and accesses grades[scores[i]]. Right approach uses a smaller array grades[11] = {'F','D','C','B','A','A'} with arithmetic conversion. Students must fill in the index expression and the if/else condition.
notes_text: This combines multiple concepts: sequential access through the scores array, random access into the grades array, and an arithmetic conversion (scores[i]/10 - 5) to map scores to grade indices. The if statement handles the special case of scores below 60.

images.description: Two code panels showing alternative approaches to grade mapping, with grade scale shown in a side box

title: A Final Problem Solution: Grade Mapping
summary: Shows solutions: direct lookup with grades[scores[i]/10] using 11-element array, or arithmetic conversion scores[i]/10 - 5 with 6-element array plus boundary check.
main_text: The solution shows two approaches. Left: using a full 11-element grades array {'F','F','F','F','F','F','D','C','B','A','A'}, access with grades[scores[i]/10] since scores[i]/10 for a 10-point quiz gives 0-10 directly. Right: using a smaller grades array {'F','D','C','B','A','A'} with an if-else: if(scores[i] < 60) idx = 'F'; else idx = scores[i] / 10 - 5; then access grades[mygr]. The arithmetic scores[i]/10 - 5 maps: 60s->1 (D), 70s->2 (C), 80s->3 (B), 90s->4 (A), 100->5 (A). Scores below 60 are handled by the if branch.
notes_text: Both solutions are valid. The first is simpler but uses more memory. The second is more memory-efficient but requires a conditional. This illustrates a common design tradeoff in programming.

images.description: Two completed code panels showing both grade mapping solutions with grade scale reference

title: Sequential vs Random Access Review
summary: Summary comparison of when to use sequential access (visit every element) versus random access (visit one element) with common task examples for each.
main_text: Sequential: Use sequential access when you MUST or MAY POTENTIALLY need to visit EVERY element. Common tasks: Combining ALL elements (sum or average, count-if e.g. count how many 100s, modify-all e.g. increment all). Search/select an element potentially stopping (break) early in an unsorted array (find a particular value, minimum/maximum). Random-Access: Use random access when you only need to visit 1 element. Common tasks: As a look-up table (for conversions from integers to other types, for substitutions where relationships/patterns between input and output are hard to express). Counting, frequency analysis, histograms.
notes_text: This summary slide consolidates all the array access pattern concepts. Students should be able to identify which pattern a problem requires by asking: Do I need to look at all elements, or can I compute a single index? This is a fundamental algorithmic thinking skill.

title: Digging Deeper: Arguments and the Stack Section Header
summary: Section divider for a deeper look at how pass-by-value and pass-by-reference work at the memory/stack level.
main_text: This section provides a deeper look at HOW pass-by-value and pass-by-reference work at the memory level, specifically examining the system stack. Understanding stack mechanics explains why arguments are copies (pass-by-value) and how array addresses enable pass-by-reference behavior.
notes_text: This section moves from the conceptual/analogy level to the actual memory implementation. Understanding the stack is important for debugging, understanding recursion, and knowing why certain programming patterns work the way they do.

title: Memory Organization: RAM Layout of a Program
summary: Describes the four main regions of a program's memory: Code, Global Data, Heap, and Stack, with focus on the stack for function data.
main_text: Programs use a 32-bit address range (0x0 to 0xffffffff). Note 0x indicates a hexadecimal number. Code usually sits at lower addresses. Global variables/data sit somewhere after code. Heap is an area of memory that can be allocated and de-allocated during program execution (i.e. dynamically at run-time) based on the needs of the program -- more in a few lectures. Stack (our focus): Memory for all information related to each running instance of a function, including: arguments to the function, local variables, and return link (where in the code to return). The memory layout diagram shows from bottom to top: Code (at 0x00000000), Global Data (at 0x10000000), Heap, Stack (at 0xc0000000, growing downward), Mapped I/O, up to 0xffffffff.
notes_text: This is foundational systems knowledge. The stack grows downward in memory while the heap grows upward. Each function call creates a new stack frame containing its local variables, arguments, and return address. When the function returns, its stack frame is deallocated.

images.description: Vertical memory layout diagram showing Code at bottom (0x00000000), Global Data (0x10000000), Heap, Stack (0xc0000000 with downward arrow), Mapped I/O, ending at 0xffffffff

title: Mapping of Info to Memory: Code Example
summary: Shows how a factorial program's global variables, function arguments, and local variables map to different regions of memory.
main_text: A code example illustrates how different parts of a program map to memory regions. The program includes: global variable int timesCalled = 0 (stored in Global Data at 0x10000000), function factorial(int n) with argument n (stored on Stack at 0xc0000000) and local variable int f (also on Stack), and main() with local variables int n, int res (on Stack). The memory layout shows Code at bottom, Global Data storing timesCalled, Heap in the middle, and Stack at top storing function arguments and local variables. Dashed arrows connect code elements to their memory locations.
notes_text: This concrete example helps students visualize where their variables actually live in memory. Global variables persist for the program's lifetime, while local variables and arguments only exist while their function is executing on the stack.

images.description: Code listing with arrows pointing to memory layout diagram, showing where global variables, arguments, and local variables are stored in Code, Global Data, Heap, and Stack regions

title: Understanding the Stack and Pass-by-Value
summary: Shows how the system stack allocates separate memory frames for each function call, with arguments copied into the new frame.
main_text: Each program allocates an area of memory known as the system stack where all data related to the function is stored including: local variables, arguments to the function, and return link (where to return) to the calling code. Each time a function is called, the computer allocates memory for that function on the top of the stack and creates a link for where to return. When a function returns/ends, that memory is deallocated (destroying all arguments and local variables) and control is returned to the function now on top. The stack diagram shows: main's frame at 0xbf8-0xbfc with y=3 and return link 00400120, and dec's frame at 0xbf0-0xbf4 with y=2 (the copy, decremented) and return link 00400ca0. The code shows main calling dec(y), and dec's y being a separate copy.
notes_text: This is a starred/important slide. The stack visualization makes pass-by-value concrete: main's y at address 0xbf8 holds 3, while dec's y at address 0xbf0 holds a copy that gets decremented to 2. They are at different memory addresses and completely independent.

images.description: Stack diagram showing two frames: main (y=3, return link) at lower addresses and dec (y=2, return link) at higher addresses. Code listing with arrows showing execution flow.

title: Understanding the Stack: Arguments Always Copied
summary: Reinforces that arguments are ALWAYS copied into the new function's stack area, showing the fixed version with return value.
main_text: Arguments are ALWAYS copied into the new function's area on the stack. The corrected code changes dec to return int and uses y = dec(y) in main. The stack diagram shows: main's frame with y=3 at 0xbf8 (later updated to 2), and dec's frame with y=2 at 0xbf0 and return value 2. The arrows show the return value 2 being passed back to main, where y = dec(y) captures it and overwrites main's y from 3 to 2. This demonstrates the correct way to communicate results back from a function using return values.
notes_text: This is the solution to the motivating question from slide 3. By changing void dec to int dec with return y, and capturing the result with y = dec(y), the value is correctly communicated back. The copy mechanism remains -- the difference is that the return value creates a new copy going back to the caller.

images.description: Stack diagram showing dec's frame with y=2 and return value 2, main's frame with y being updated from 3 to 2 via the return value. Code shows corrected version with int dec returning y.

title: Scope and Stack Example: Multiple Function Calls
summary: Demonstrates scope and stack with three nested function calls (main, avg, printAv) showing how each gets its own stack frame with independent variables.
main_text: The scope of local variables and arguments are only for the lifetime of the function in which they live. One function cannot access the local variables of another. The example shows main calling avg(x,y) which calls printAv(sum). Three stack frames are shown simultaneously: main's frame (0xbf0-0xbfc) with x=6, y=9, z=-1.05/7.5, and return link. avg's frame (0xbe0-0xbec) with n1=6, n2=9, sum=7.5, and return link. printAv's frame (0xbe8-0xbec) with av=7.5 and return link. cout's frame at the top. The code includes prototypes for avg and printAv, main calling both, and the function definitions.
notes_text: This multi-level stack example shows that each function call creates a completely independent frame. Even though printAv's av and avg's sum both hold 7.5, they are separate copies at different memory addresses. The scope rules prevent any function from directly reading another's local variables.

images.description: Stack diagram showing four frames (cout, printAv, avg, main) with memory addresses and variable values. Code listing shows the complete program with prototypes, main, avg, and printAv functions.

title: Another Stack Example: avg Function Execution
summary: Shows the stack state during avg(x,y) execution with n1=6, n2=9, sum=15, demonstrating how values flow through the stack.
main_text: Each program allocates an area of memory known as the system stack where all data related to the function is stored including: local variables, arguments to the function, and return link (where to return) to the calling code. This example shows the stack during the first call to avg(x,y). The avg frame contains: n1=6 at 0xbe0, n2=9 at 0xbe4, sum=15 at 0xbe8, and return link 00400ca0 at 0xbec. Main's frame contains: x=6 at 0xbf0, y=9 at 0xbf4, z=-1.05 (then updated to 7.5) at 0xbf8, and return link 00400120 at 0xbfc. The avg function computes sum = n1 + n2 = 15 and returns sum/2.0 = 7.5.
notes_text: This concrete stack trace helps students trace through code execution. Note that z initially contains garbage (-1.05) before being assigned the return value of avg. The return link addresses show where execution resumes after each function returns.

images.description: Stack diagram showing avg frame (n1=6, n2=9, sum=15) and main frame (x=6, y=9, z=7.5) with code listing of the avg function

title: The Stack and Arrays Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing how arrays interact with the stack, including how array addresses are passed on the stack.
main_text: This section examines how arrays are represented on the stack and how passing an array's starting address on the stack enables pass-by-reference behavior for arrays.
notes_text: This section connects the stack concepts from the previous section with the array pass-by-reference behavior described earlier, providing the complete picture of how array arguments work at the memory level.

title: Array Element Addresses: Train Car Analogy
summary: Uses a train car analogy to derive the formula for computing the memory address of any array element based on starting address, index, and element size.
main_text: Consider a train with many copies of the same car. The 0th car starts at point A on the number line, and each car is 5 meters long. Write an arithmetic expression for where the i-th car is located (at what meter on the number line does it start). The answer is A + 5*i. Similarly, suppose an array of integers starts at memory address A, write an expression for where the i-th integer starts. Since int is 4 bytes, the answer is A + 4*i. Suppose an array of doubles starts at memory address A, write an expression for where the i-th double starts. Since double is 8 bytes, the answer is A + 8*i. The general formula for the address of the i-th element is: start_address + i * element_size.
notes_text: The train analogy makes the address calculation intuitive. Each car/element is the same size, so the offset is simply the index times the size. This formula is what the CPU uses internally when you write array[i] in code. Students should fill in the blanks themselves.

images.description: Train cars on a number line showing 0th car at A, 1st car at A+5, 2nd car at A+10. Three blank formula boxes for students to fill in.
labels: Formula for address of i-th element:

title: Array Elements vs Array Names: Fun Fact 3
summary: Key concept: using an array name without brackets evaluates to the starting address of the array, not its data. vals[0] gives data, vals gives an address.
main_text: Fun Fact 3 (after Unit 0's Fun Fact 1 and 2): In C/C++, using an array name without any index evaluates to the starting address of the array. For example, vals yields an address while vals[0] yields data. The code shows int vals[5] = {7,4,9,2,3} at address 0x7420. cout << vals[0] prints 7 (data). cout << vals prints the address (e.g. 0x7420), not the array contents. To get data, you must supply an index. Fun Fact 3b: Fun Fact 3 usually appears as one of the first few questions on the midterm.
notes_text: This is a critical concept that confuses many students. The array name IS a pointer to the first element. This is why arrays are passed by reference -- passing the array name passes its address. The table shows vals at address 0x7420 with values 7,4,9,2,3 at indices [0]-[4].

images.description: Table showing array vals at address 0x7420 with indices [0]-[4] and values 7,4,9,2,3. Code example and info box about Fun Fact 3.

title: Formula for Addressing Array Elements
summary: Shows the concrete formula start_addr + i*data_size for computing element addresses, and warns that C/C++ does NOT perform bounds checking.
main_text: Assume a 5-element int array: int x[5] = {8,5,3,9,6}; starting at address 7400. When you access x[2], the CPU uses x (to know the starting address) and adds the product of the index 2 times the size of the data type (int = 4 bytes). x[2] => int at address 7400 + 2*4 = 7408. x[3] => int at address 7400 + 3*4 = 7412. General formula: x[i] at start address of array + i * (size of int). To access an element in an array, we need 3 pieces of info: 1) Start address of the array, 2) Index/offset, 3) Type of elements (really the size of that type). Formula: start_addr + i*data_size. Recall: C/C++ does NOT perform bounds checking to stop you from attempting to access an element beyond the end of the array. x[6] => int at address 7400 + 6*4 = 7424 -- this is Garbage since the array only has indices 0-4!
notes_text: The memory table shows addresses 7400-7424 with actual hex values. Accessing x[6] goes to address 7424 which contains whatever happens to be in memory there (a184beef feedface) -- this is undefined behavior and a major source of bugs and security vulnerabilities.

images.description: Memory table showing addresses 7400-7424 with array values and beyond-array garbage. Info box listing 3 pieces needed for array access with formula.

title: Recall: Passing Arrays - Address as Link
summary: Reiterates that when passing arrays, only the starting address (pointer) is passed, and the function uses address, type, and index to access elements.
main_text: The 'link' that is passed is just the starting address of (pointer to) the array in memory (e.g. 7420). Once the function has the start address and the type, it will produce its own index values and be able to access the array in the caller's memory. The code shows int sum(int data[], int size) receiving the address 7420 for the vals array. The diagram shows main's vals array at addresses 7420-7816, with data in sum() receiving just the address value 7420 as a disk/pointer icon. The three pieces of info needed to access an element are: 1) Start address, 2) Index/offset, 3) Type of elements (size of that type).
notes_text: This slide revisits the earlier concept but now with the stack and memory address knowledge. The data parameter in sum() holds the value 7420, which is the memory address of vals[0] in main's stack frame. Using this address plus the index and type size, sum can access any element.

images.description: Diagram showing main's vals array with address 7420 being passed as a pointer value to sum's data parameter. Code listing and info box about array access requirements.

title: Stack View of Passing Arrays: init() Function
summary: Shows the stack layout when passing an array to init(), demonstrating how the address 7420 in init's frame points back to main's vals array.
main_text: The function receives the starting address of the array which it can use along with the type (e.g. int) and index to access the appropriate values from main's stack area of memory. The stack diagram shows: init's frame at addresses 7400-7412 with i (iterating 0-99), data=7420 (the address of vals), size=100, and return link. Main's frame at 7416-7820 with mysum=0, vals[0] through vals[99] at addresses 7420-7816, and return link. Step 1: We copy the address as init()'s argument, not the values. Step 2: The address allows init() to access the original data in main(). The init function sets data[i] = 5 for all i, which modifies vals directly since data points to the same memory.
notes_text: This is a starred/important slide showing the complete stack picture. The key insight is that data in init()'s frame holds 7420 -- the same address where vals[0] lives in main's frame. When init writes to data[i], it's writing to address 7420 + i*4, which IS vals[i].

images.description: Detailed stack diagram showing init's frame with data=7420 pointer and main's frame with vals array at address 7420. Arrows show how data[i] in init accesses vals[i] in main.
