title: Why Empty Brackets in Array Parameters
summary: Explains why array parameters use empty brackets (int data[]) rather than specifying a size, for generality since C/C++ does not bounds check anyway.
main_text: Why don't we just supply the array size in the formal argument? C/C++ doesn't do bounds checking anyway, so what good would writing 100 be? And why would we want to limit this function to only working with arrays of size 100? Let's let it be general. The code contrasts int sum(int data[100], int size) (restrictive) with int sum(int data[], int size) (general). The stack diagram shows sum's frame with i, total=500, data=7420, size=100, and return link. Main's frame has mysum=0, vals[0]-vals[99]. Using empty brackets allows the same function to work with arrays of any size, making the code reusable.
notes_text: The circled 100 in int data[100] highlights this as a bad practice. Since C/C++ ignores the size in brackets for function parameters anyway (it still just passes the address), specifying it adds no safety and reduces generality. The size parameter serves the purpose of communicating array length.

images.description: Stack diagram showing sum's frame accessing main's vals array via address 7420. Code comparison highlighting int data[100] (bad) vs int data[] (good).

title: Array Summary: Key Facts
summary: Summarizes array rules: fixed size declaration, C/C++ only remembers start address and type, no bounds checking, and the address formula.
main_text: Arrays must be declared with a FIXED size (cannot use a variable for its length). GOOD: int data[50]; BAD: int data[n]; After declaring an array, C/C++ only 'remembers' the starting address of the array and the type of data it holds (to know the data size). Which is all it needs to know to access any element using the formula: start_addr + i*data_size. C/C++ do NO bounds checking. They will simply apply the formula above to WHATEVER index you provide or calculate. This is the most common source of a program crash (and also security vulnerabilities). If your program crashes in CS 103, suspect a bad array access.
notes_text: This is a crucial summary slide. The three key takeaways: 1) Arrays have fixed size at compile time, 2) Only address and type are stored (no length!), 3) No bounds checking means out-of-bounds access causes crashes or security vulnerabilities. Students should always validate indices before using them.

title: C-Strings, cout, and cin Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing C-strings and their special relationship with cout and cin for input/output operations.
main_text: This section covers C-strings (character arrays) and how cout and cin have special behavior when working with character arrays compared to other array types. C-strings are fundamental to understanding text processing in C/C++.
notes_text: C-strings are a legacy from C that are still widely used in C++. Understanding them is important because many system APIs and libraries use them, and they reveal how strings actually work at the memory level.

title: Character Arrays and Strings (1): C-String Basics
summary: Explains that C/C++ string constants are character arrays terminated by the null character '\0', and shows how to declare, initialize, modify, and I/O them.
main_text: In C/C++, string constants (text between double quotes) are just character arrays. Each character consumes 1 element in the array. They end with the null character (0 decimal or '\0' ASCII). This approach of using an array of chars to store a string is referred to as a C-String because there was no string type in C (before C++). The code demonstrates: char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'} and char str2[7] = "CS 103" (initializes the array to 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0'). cout << str1 prints "CS", cout << str2 prints "CS 103". str2[5] = '4' changes the string to "CS 104". cin >> str2 with input "hello" replaces the contents. The memory layout shows str2 at addresses 520-526 containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0'.
notes_text: The null terminator '\0' is critical -- it tells functions like cout where the string ends. Without it, cout would keep reading memory past the array boundary. The string literal "CS 103" automatically includes the null terminator, which is why str2 needs 7 characters (6 for text + 1 for null).

images.description: Memory layout showing str2 at addresses 520-526 with characters 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0'. Code example with output showing string operations.

title: Character Arrays and Loops: How cout Handles Strings
summary: Shows that cout internally loops through character arrays until the null terminator, while other arrays require manual loops for printing.
main_text: How many things can a computer do at a time? One. To print out a string/character array, we would have to print one character at a time. But C/C++ treats character arrays specially. cout has a loop inside its code to print strings/character arrays. Similarly, cin has a loop inside to input a string. We say cout and cin have a special relationship with character arrays. The code shows manual printing with a for loop: for(int i=0; str[i] != '\0'; i++) { cout << str[i]; } But you can simply write: cout << str1; and cout will automatically loop through all characters until it hits '\0'. The memory layout shows str1 containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0' and program output shows both approaches produce the same result.
notes_text: This explains the magic behind cout << str working for character arrays. cout checks if it receives a char* (character pointer/array) and if so, loops character by character until hitting null. For other array types like int[], cout just prints the address, which is why you need manual loops.

images.description: Memory layout of str1 with characters and null terminator. Code showing manual loop vs direct cout output producing identical results.

title: cout's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Demonstrates that cout treats character arrays specially by printing all characters, while for other array types it prints the address or requires manual loops.
main_text: To print out all elements of any array type OTHER than a character array (int, double, bool, etc.) you must write your OWN loop because computers can only do 1 thing at a time. But for character arrays, you can just give cout the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to print out all characters for you. So internally it is actually looping over the characters, so you do not have to. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to print out all the characters. Thus, we say cout treats character arrays specially. The code shows: for int array, you must loop and print each element. cout << data prints the address (0x7fffce40), not the values. But cout << str1 prints "Many chars". Program output: 9 7 8 9 5 / 0x7fffce40 / Many chars.
notes_text: This is a common source of confusion. When students write cout << intArray, they expect to see the values but get a hex address instead. Only character arrays get the special treatment of printing actual content. This behavior is inherited from C's printf with %s format specifier.

images.description: Two array tables: data[5] = {9,7,8,9,5} and str1 = 'Many chars'. Code showing different cout behavior for int vs char arrays. Program output demonstrates the difference.

title: cin's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Shows that cin treats character arrays specially by reading a full word into the array, while other array types require manual element-by-element input.
main_text: To get input for all elements of an array type OTHER than character arrays (int, double, etc.) you must write your OWN loop. But for character arrays, you can just give cin the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to receive all the characters the user types and store them sequentially in the array. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to get a full string (stopping at the next space). cin treats character arrays specially. The code shows: cin >> data won't even compile for int arrays. For int input, use a loop: for(int i=0; i<5; i++) cin >> data[i]. But cin >> str1 reads an entire word at once. When user types 'CS102', cin stores 'C','S','1','0','2','\0' into str1 automatically, including the null terminator.
notes_text: cin stops reading at whitespace for character arrays. It also automatically appends the null terminator. However, cin does NOT check if the input fits in the array, which leads to buffer overflow problems discussed on the next slide.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing str1 before cin (garbage values) and after cin with 'CS102' input: 'C','S','1','0','2','\0' stored with null terminator.

title: Buffer Overflow: cin and Character Arrays
summary: Warns that cin does not check array bounds, so input longer than the array overwrites adjacent memory, causing crashes or security vulnerabilities.
main_text: What if the user types in TOO much (more characters than our array has room to store)? cin will not stop! It will keep storing the characters the user types, overwriting whatever data and variables came after the array. Warning: cin does not CHECK that the string typed by the user will fit in the array; instead it simply overwrites memory leading to undefined (bad) behavior! The example shows char str1[4] with int sum = 0 after it. If user types 'CS102' (5 chars + null = 6 bytes), cin writes past str1's 4 bytes, overwriting sum's memory. cout << sum will not see 0 because sum was modified by the overflow. C++ strings fix this issue, allocating more space based on what is typed. Memory diagrams show str1 at addresses 520-523 with sum at 524, and after overflow str1 contains 'C','S','1','0' with '3','\0' overwriting sum.
notes_text: Buffer overflow is one of the most dangerous and common security vulnerabilities in C/C++. It is the basis for many hacker exploits. C++ string objects dynamically resize and are immune to this problem, which is why modern C++ prefers std::string over C-strings.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing str1[4] and sum before and after buffer overflow from cin input 'CS103'. The overflow overwrites sum's memory location.

title: C-Strings (Character Arrays) Operations Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing operations on C-strings (NULL terminated character arrays) including comparison, copying, and concatenation.
main_text: This section covers operations that can be performed on C-strings (NULL terminated character arrays), including the limitations of using standard operators and the library functions provided to work with them.
notes_text: Unlike C++ string objects which support operators like ==, =, and +, C-strings require special library functions for these operations. Understanding why standard operators fail on C-strings requires understanding that arrays are addresses, not values.

title: C-Strings: No Standard Operators
summary: Explains that C-strings do not support comparison (==), assignment (=), or concatenation (+) operators because arrays are addresses, not values.
main_text: In C, strings were not a first-class type (i.e. no string type). Strings were simply character arrays (char[]) terminated by the null character (0 dec. = '\0' ASCII). These were known as C-Strings. No operations/operators other than typical array operations are provided: No comparison (== or !=), No assignment/copy (=), No append/concatenate (+). The code shows attempting these operations: if(str3 == str1) actually compares addresses, not contents. str3 = str1 and str3 += str2 will not compile because array types are not assignable. The memory shows str1 at address 800 containing 'C','S','1','0','3',' ','i','s',' ','\0'.
notes_text: This is a key gotcha for students coming from Python or Java. In those languages, == compares string content. In C/C++ with char arrays, == compares memory addresses (pointers), which is almost never what you want. The compiler may warn about this but it is a common mistake.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str1 at address 800 with C-string contents. Code attempting to use ==, =, and += on C-strings.

title: C-String Errors: Compiler Warnings and Errors
summary: Shows actual compiler errors when attempting to use ==, =, and += on C-strings, demonstrating that these operations fail or behave incorrectly.
main_text: The code attempts three operations on C-strings that fail: 1) if(str3 == str1) generates a compiler warning: 'comparison between two arrays is deprecated; array comparison always evaluates to false'. This compares addresses, not string content. 2) str3 = str1 generates error: 'array type char[15] is not assignable'. Arrays cannot be assigned with =. 3) str3 += str2 generates error: 'invalid operands to binary expression (char[15] and char[7])'. The += operator does not work on arrays. Memory diagrams show str1 at address 800 ('CS103 is '), str2 at 820 ('fun'), and str3 at 840 ('cool' from user input via cin). The compiler output explicitly shows these errors.
notes_text: Showing actual compiler error messages helps students understand what goes wrong and learn to interpret error output. The deprecated warning on == is particularly insidious because it compiles (possibly with just a warning) but gives the wrong result, while = and += are hard errors.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing three C-strings in memory. Compiler error output showing warnings and errors for ==, =, and += operations.

title: C String Function Library: strlen, strcmp, strcpy, strcat
summary: Introduces the cstring library functions for C-string operations: strlen (length), strcmp (compare), strcpy (copy), and strcat (concatenate).
main_text: A library of functions was provided to perform operations on character arrays representing strings (<cstring> in C++, <string.h> in C). int strlen(char dest[]): Returns the length of the string (not counting the null character). int strcmp(char str1[], char str2[]): Returns 0 if equal, >0 if str1 is alphanumerically larger than str2, <0 if str1 is less than str2. char* strcpy(char dest[], char src[]): Copies the whole C-string from src to the dest array (overwriting what's in dest). Ignore the return type for now (think of it as a void function). char* strcat(char dest[], char src[]): Concatenates src to the end of dest. Ignore the return type for now (think of it as a void function).
notes_text: These four functions are the C-string equivalents of .length(), ==, =, and + for C++ strings. They all work by iterating through characters until hitting the null terminator. Students should memorize these function signatures and understand that dest must have enough space for the result.

title: Use of the C-String Library: Complete Example
summary: Demonstrates practical use of strcmp, strcpy, and strcat to compare, copy, and concatenate C-strings, replacing the invalid ==, =, and += operators.
main_text: The code includes <cstring> and shows correct C-string operations: str1[] = "CS103 is ", str2[] = "fun", str3[15] is read from cin (user enters 'cool'). Instead of str3 == str1, use: if(0 == strcmp(str1, str3)) { cout << "Match"; }. Instead of str3 = str1, use: strcpy(str3, str1); -- this copies 'CS103 is ' into str3. Memory shows str3 at 840 now contains 'C','S','1','0','3',' ','i','s',' ','\0'. Instead of str3 += str2, use: strcat(str3, str2); -- this appends 'fun' to str3. Memory shows str3 at 840 now contains 'C','S','1','0','3',' ','i','s',' ','f','u','n','\0'. The final cout << str3 prints "CS103 is fun".
notes_text: This example shows the correct replacements for all three failed operations from slide 58. Note that strcmp returns 0 for equal strings (counterintuitive), so the comparison is if(0 == strcmp(...)). strcpy and strcat both require the destination to have enough space, or buffer overflow occurs.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing str1, str2, and str3 at addresses 800, 820, 840 through the stages of strcpy and strcat operations. Code listing with correct C-string function calls.

title: Sample Implementations: strlen and strcpy Exercises
summary: Presents exercises for students to implement strlen and strcpy functions themselves to understand how C-string functions work internally.
main_text: This slide presents exercises for students to implement two fundamental C-string functions: strlen (string length) and strcpy (string copy). Implementing these functions helps students understand how C-string library functions work internally by iterating through characters until the null terminator is found. strlen counts characters until '\0' is reached. strcpy copies characters one by one from source to destination until '\0' is copied.
notes_text: These implementation exercises reinforce that C-string functions are essentially loops that process characters until the null terminator. strlen increments a counter while the current character is not '\0'. strcpy copies each character from src to dest and stops after copying '\0'.

title: Cipher Exercise: Array as Lookup Table for Encryption
summary: Exercise using a character array as a lookup table to implement a substitution cipher for encrypting text.
main_text: Cipher: Using an array as a Look-Up Table. Create a cipher code to encrypt text. The standard alphabet abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz maps to the cipher ghijklmaefnzyqbcdrstuopvwx. Given char orig_string[] = "helloworld" and char new_string[11], after encryption new_string should be "akzzbpbrzj". Define another array: char cipher[27] = "ghijklmaefnzyqbcdrstuopvwx". The question is: how could we use the original character to index ('look up' a value in) the cipher array? The key insight is that subtracting 'a' from a lowercase letter gives its 0-based position (e.g., 'h'-'a' = 7), which can be used as an index into the cipher array.
notes_text: This exercise combines multiple concepts: character arrays, ASCII arithmetic (subtracting 'a' to get 0-based index), and arrays as lookup tables. The conversion cipher[orig_string[i] - 'a'] maps each character through the substitution table. This is a practical application of random access.

title: Input Buffer Overflow: Stack Corruption Example
summary: Demonstrates how cin input longer than the array corrupts the stack, overwriting local variables like size and loc, leading to crashes.
main_text: Depending on user input, this program will likely crash. The program finds the location of the first capital letter in text. It declares char str[8], const int size = 8, int loc = 0, then uses cin >> str. If the user types 'abcdefgh0123456' (more than 8 characters), cin writes past str's 8 bytes, corrupting size and loc on the stack. The stack before execution shows str at address 7300 (8 bytes of garbage), size at 7308 (value 8), loc at 7312 (value 0). After cin >> str with the long input, the ASCII values of the input overwrite everything: str gets 61-68, but size and loc are overwritten with 30-36 (ASCII for '0'-'6'). The isupper check on corrupted data produces unpredictable results.
notes_text: This is a concrete demonstration of why buffer overflow is so dangerous. The stack layout shows exactly how local variables after the array get overwritten. In a real attack, a hacker could craft input to overwrite the return link, hijacking program execution (covered in CS 356).

images.description: Two stack diagrams showing memory before and after cin overflow. Before: str has garbage, size=8, loc=0. After: str and subsequent variables overwritten with ASCII input values. Code listing showing the vulnerable program.

title: Solutions and More Function Examples Section Header
summary: Section divider for self-study solutions and additional function examples covering pass-by-value, array passing, and scope.
main_text: This section provides solutions to earlier exercises and additional function examples for self-study. Students are encouraged to work through these examples and ask questions about concepts that are unclear.
notes_text: The remaining slides provide solutions and reinforcement of key concepts from the unit. Students should trace through the code and stack diagrams on their own before checking the solutions.

title: Pass by Value Solution: Using Return to Communicate
summary: Shows the corrected dec function using return value to properly communicate the decremented result back to main.
main_text: Revisiting the motivating example, the original code with void dec(int y) { y--; } does not change main's y because each function is a completely separate sandbox isolated from other functions and their data, and copies of data are passed and returned between them. The only way to communicate back to main is via return. The solution changes dec to: int dec(int y) { y--; return y; } and main to: y = dec(y). Now dec returns the decremented value 2, which main captures and assigns to its own y. This properly communicates the result back through the return value mechanism.
notes_text: This solution reinforces the Main Point of function isolation. The sandbox analogy shows that modifications to the copy inside dec are lost unless explicitly returned. The corrected version makes dec an int function that returns the modified value.

images.description: Two code panels: original void dec version (prints 3) and corrected int dec version with return y (prints 2). Sandbox diagram showing function isolation.

title: Exercise Solution: Array Element Address Formulas
summary: Provides solutions for the train car analogy: i-th car at A + 5*i, i-th integer at A + 4*i, and i-th double at A + 8*i.
main_text: Consider a train with many copies of the same car. The 0th car starts at point A, each car is 5 meters long. The i-th car is located at A + 5*i meters. Suppose a set of integers start at memory address A, the i-th integer starts at A + 4*i (since int is 4 bytes). Suppose a set of doubles start at memory address A, the i-th double starts at A + 8*i (since double is 8 bytes). The train diagram shows 0th car at A, 1st car at A+5, 2nd car at A+10, reinforcing the general formula: start_address + index * element_size.
notes_text: These formulas are what the CPU calculates internally when you use array indexing. Understanding this helps explain why array access is O(1) -- it is just an arithmetic calculation, not a search. The element size (4 for int, 8 for double, 1 for char) determines the spacing between elements.

images.description: Train cars on number line with formulas A + 5*i, A + 4*i, and A + 8*i shown in boxes for cars, integers, and doubles respectively.

title: Parameter Passing (1): max Function Example
summary: Additional example showing formal vs actual parameters with a max function, reinforcing copy semantics and type matching.
main_text: Formal parameters a and b: Type of data the parameter expects. Names that will be used internal to the function to refer to the values passed (like 'CEO' or 'professor' in contracts that will be replaced with real values). Actual parameters: Actual values ('Jeff Bezos', 'Mark') input to the function by the caller. A copy is made and given to the function. The code shows int max(int a, int b) with if(a > b) return a; else return b; In main, int x=6, z; z = max(x, 4) passes x (value 6) and literal 4 as actuals. The formals a and b receive copies 6 and 4. The function returns 6. Each type is a different shape (int = triangle, double = square, char = circle). Only a value of that type can fit as a parameter.
notes_text: This reinforces the formal/actual parameter distinction with a different function example. The max function demonstrates how return communicates results back. The shape analogy for types (triangle=int) helps visualize type safety.

images.description: Diagram showing actuals x=6 and literal 4 being copied into formals a and b in max() sandbox, with return value 6. Code listing shows max function and main.

title: Scope Example: Global vs Local Variables and Shadowing
summary: Comprehensive scope example showing global variables, local variables, block scope, and variable shadowing with the scope resolution operator.
main_text: Globals live as long as the program is running. Variables declared in a block { ... } live as long as the block has not completed, whether that block is a function, a loop, an if statement, etc. When variables share the same name, the closest declaration will be used by default. The code shows: global int x = 5, main declares int a, x = 8, y = 3. Inside a for loop, int j = 1 is local to the loop block. cout << 'x = ' << x prints 8 (local x shadows global). The doit function takes int x, decrements it, and returns it, operating on its own copy. a = doit(y) passes y=3. cout << 'a=' << a prints 2 (doit returned 3-1=2). cout << 'y=' << y prints 3 (unchanged, pass-by-value). cout << 'glob. X' << ::x prints 5 (scope resolution operator accesses global x). Memory shows globals at low addresses (x=5), main's frame at high addresses (a=2, x=8, y=3).
notes_text: This example combines many scope concepts: global vs local, block scope for loop variables, variable shadowing (local x=8 hides global x=5), and the scope resolution operator (::x) to explicitly access the global. Students should trace through this carefully.

images.description: Code listing with scope annotations and memory layout showing Code, Globals (x=5), Heap, and Stack (main: a=2, x=8, y=3)

title: Recall: Passing Arrays As Arguments - Syntax
summary: Reviews the syntax for passing arrays as function arguments: empty brackets in prototype/definition, array name as actual parameter.
main_text: Syntax for passing arrays: Step 1: In the prototype and function definition, put empty square brackets [] after the formal parameter name if it is an array (e.g. int data[]). Alternatively, put an * between the type and formal parameter name (e.g. int* data). We prefer int data[] for now but int* data is JUST AS VALID and we will learn more about it when we cover pointers. Step 2: When you call the function, just provide the name of the array as the actual parameter. The code shows: int init(int data[], int max_size); as the prototype. In main: int vals[100]; int len = init(vals, 100); The init function reads numbers from cin into the array, stopping when the array is full or user enters -1, and returns the count of elements read.
notes_text: This slide provides a practical template for writing functions that take arrays. The init function demonstrates a common pattern: reading input into an array with a maximum size guard, using a sentinel value (-1) to stop, and returning the actual count of elements stored.

images.description: Code listing showing array function prototype with empty brackets, main function calling init with array name, and init implementation reading from cin.

title: Arrays And Pass-by-Reference: Modifications Visible to Caller
summary: Reinforces that arrays are passed by reference via addresses, so modifications in a called function are visible to the caller.
main_text: Arrays are passed-by-reference. Links (addresses) are passed. These links are actually memory addresses where the array starts. Using these addresses, any function can go to those locations and modify the data (array) from another function. It need not be returned since the function is modifying the original. Thus, changes to the array by a function are visible upon return to the caller. The code shows void init(int data[], int size) setting nums[i] = -1 for all elements. In main, int vals[10] at address 7420 is declared and init(vals, 10) is called. After init returns, cout << vals[2] prints -1, confirming that init modified main's array directly. In this example, nums and vals refer to the same array.
notes_text: This is the complete picture: the formal parameter nums in init is just another name for the same memory that vals occupies in main. Any write through nums[i] = -1 directly writes to vals[i] because they share the same starting address 7420.

images.description: Code showing init function setting all elements to -1 and main verifying the changes. Array visualization showing vals with all -1 values at address 7420.

title: Lack of Array Bounds Checking: Security Implications
summary: Warns that C++ does NOT bounds check array accesses, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes that corrupt stack data and enable hacker exploits.
main_text: C++ does NOT bounds check the index used to access an element. It will simply treat all of memory as part of the array (larger positive indices go past the end, negative offsets go before the array start). This means you could potentially read and write data you should not (including variables from your own function or another function since local variables live on the stack). This issue is a common exploit by hackers (more in future courses like CS 356). The example shows int f1() with int dat[4], x=0. The loop for(int i=0; i <= 4; i++) has an off-by-one error (should be i < 4, not i <= 4). When i=4, dat[4] writes to what is actually x's memory location (since x is adjacent on the stack at address 7436). The input values 9,4,3,7,1000 cause dat[4]=1000 which overwrites x, so cout << x prints 1000 instead of 0. Accessing dat[1000] would likely cause a segmentation fault.
notes_text: This is one of the most important security lessons in the course. Off-by-one errors (using <= instead of <) are extremely common and can overwrite critical stack data including return addresses. In CS 356, students learn how attackers exploit this to inject malicious code.

images.description: Stack diagram showing f1's frame with dat[0-3] at addresses 7420-7432, x at 7436, and return link at 7440. dat[4] at 7436 overlaps with x, and writing 1000 there corrupts x.

title: Stack View of Passing Arrays: sum() Function
summary: Complete stack diagram showing sum() accessing main's vals array through the passed starting address, with init having already set all values to 5.
main_text: The function receives the starting address of the array which it can use along with the type (e.g. int) and index to access the appropriate values from main's stack area of memory. The stack diagram shows two stages: sum's frame at addresses 7396-7412 with i (iterating 0-99), total (accumulating to 500), data=7420, size=100, and return link. Main's frame at 7416-7820 with mysum (updated from 0 to 500), vals[0]-vals[99] (all containing 5 from init). The code shows void init(int data[], int size) and int sum(int data[], int size) prototypes. Main calls init(vals, 100) then mysum = sum(vals, 100). sum iterates through the array using the address 7420, accumulating total = 5*100 = 500, which is returned and stored in mysum.
notes_text: This final stack diagram ties together all the concepts: function stack frames, pass-by-value for size (100 is copied), pass-by-reference for arrays (address 7420 points to main's data), and the address formula for accessing elements (7420 + 4*i). The expression 7420+4*i is shown explicitly for the element access.

images.description: Detailed stack diagram showing sum's frame (i, total=500, data=7420, size=100) accessing main's vals array (all 5s). Arrows show data[i] accessing vals[i] through address 7420+4*i. Code listing shows both init and sum functions.
